# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered rare and untreatable, CA is now recognized as an increasingly diagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), driven by advances in noninvasive imaging and the advent of disease-modifying therapies [1,2]. The two predominant forms affecting the heart are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, which itself comprises hereditary (ATTRv) and wild-type (ATTRwt) subtypes [3].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

ATTRwt amyloidosis is far more common than previously appreciated, identified in up to 13% of patients hospitalized with HFpEF and in a substantial fraction of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis [4,5]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing toxic light chains, leading to rapid cardiac deterioration if untreated [6]. In ATTR, destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer—either through aging (ATTRwt) or pathogenic point mutations (ATTRv)—promotes monomer dissociation and fibril formation [7]. The Val122Ile (V142I) variant is notably prevalent among individuals of African ancestry and confers increased risk of cardiomyopathy [8].

## Clinical Presentation

CA should be suspected in older patients with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, HFpEF, low-voltage electrocardiograms despite increased wall thickness, and discordant findings between imaging and ECG [9]. Extracardiac "red flags" are particularly useful: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic dysfunction frequently precede the cardiac diagnosis by years [10,11]. AL amyloidosis may additionally manifest with nephrotic-range proteinuria, periorbital purpura, and macroglossia [6].

## Diagnosis

The diagnostic paradigm has been transformed by noninvasive testing. Echocardiography typically reveals increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic reduction in longitudinal strain with apical sparing ("cherry-on-top" pattern) [12]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [13]. A landmark contribution has been bone scintigraphy using technetium-labeled tracers (e.g., 99mTc-PYP, DPD, HMDP), which permits diagnosis of ATTR-CA without endomyocardial biopsy when monoclonal protein is excluded by serum and urine immunofixation and free light-chain assay [14,15]. Grade 2–3 myocardial uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein has a specificity approaching 100% for ATTR-CA [14]. When AL is suspected or scintigraphy is equivocal, tissue confirmation with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry–based typing remains essential [16].

## Treatment

Management of AL-CA centers on rapidly suppressing the plasma cell clone. Regimens incorporating bortezomib, and more recently the addition of daratumumab, have improved hematologic and organ responses [17,18]. Autologous stem cell transplantation benefits carefully selected patients [6]. For ATTR-CA, transthyretin stabilizers represent the cornerstone of therapy. Tafamidis significantly reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial [19]. Acoramidis, a newer stabilizer, demonstrated favorable clinical outcomes in the ATTRibute-CM trial [20]. Gene-silencing approaches—patisiran and inotersen—were initially approved for hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [21,22], and the CRISPR-based agent NTLA-2001 has shown durable reductions in serum TTR [23]. The APOLLO-B trial evaluated patisiran specifically in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24], while emerging data on eplontersen and vutrisiran continue to expand options [25].

General heart failure management requires caution: loop diuretics are the mainstay for congestion, whereas beta-blockers and renin-angiotensin inhibitors are often poorly tolerated due to fixed stroke volume and autonomic dysfunction [26]. Anticoagulation is frequently warranted given the high prevalence of atrial thrombi even in sinus rhythm [27].

## Prognosis and Risk Stratification

Staging systems incorporating cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP and troponin) and, for AL, the difference in free light chains, provide robust prognostic discrimination [28]. ATTR-specific staging using NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate stratifies survival in ATTR-CA [29]. Untreated AL-CA carries the worst prognosis, with median survival of months in advanced stages, underscoring the importance of early recognition [6].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from a uniformly fatal diagnosis into a treatable condition. Heightened clinical awareness, judicious use of noninvasive imaging, and timely deployment of disease-modifying therapy can substantially alter outcomes. Future directions include fibril-depleting antibodies and gene-editing strategies that may move treatment from disease stabilization toward genuine reversal [30].
